color_description: Brilliant deep blue with a slight reddish undertone; highly saturated and vivid [oai_citation_attribution:0‡colors.muz.li](https://colors.muz.li/color/ultramarine-blue#:~:text=4166F5,color%20of%20deep%20ocean%20waters).

source: Indigofera tinctoria plant leaves (for natural indigo) or coal tar (for synthetic indigo)
synthesis: Heumann's synthesis (1897) from aniline via N-phenylglycine

color_description: Intense greenish-blue (in PB15:3 form) or reddish-blue (PB15:6 form); extremely high tinting strength and excellent lightfastness.
history: Transformed modern paint palettes since the 1930s; widely used in paints, inks, plastics for its vivid color and stability (e.g., printing process cyan).
natural_sources: Phthalic anhydride, urea, copper salts in chemical reaction (accidentally discovered 1927)

color_description: Brilliant intense dark green with a blue undertone; very high tinting strength and transparency; extraordinarily lightfast.
history: Replaced older greens in virtually all applications post-1940s; staple in printing, artist paints (the ubiquitous 'phthalo green'), automotive finishes, etc.
natural_sources: Derived from phthalocyanine blue via chlorination process

color_description: Bright purple-violet dye; yields a brilliant mauve color on silk but fades with exposure to light and washing.
formula: Mixture of related purple azine salts [oai_citation_attribution:62‡en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauveine#:~:text=Mauveine%20is%20a%20mixture%20of,6)
history: The first synthetic organic dye; sparked the modern chemical industry; fashionable in the late 1850s but quickly superseded by more robust dyes [oai_citation_attribution:66‡edu.rsc.org](https://edu.rsc.org/feature/the-battle-for-magenta/2020242.article#:~:text=Three%20years%20after%20the%20discovery,and%20is%20still%20used%20today).
natural_sources: Synthesized from aniline (coal tar) and potassium dichromate oxidizer [oai_citation_attribution:63‡en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauveine#:~:text=Mauveine%20is%20a%20mixture%20of,6)
not_used_reason: No (fugitive; replaced by more durable dyes soon after discovery)
source: Coal tar aniline dye (mixture of aromatic compounds)
synthesis: Perkin's accidental oxidation of aniline (1856) [oai_citation_attribution:64‡en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauveine#:~:text=Mauveine%2C%20also%20known%20as%20aniline,produced.%5B%204%20%5D%5B%205)

color_description: Brilliant purplish-red (hot pink) dye; much more lightfast than mauveine and can be made into a lake pigment for inks.
history: Second synthetic dye after mauve; named 'Magenta' for a battle in 1859 [oai_citation_attribution:70‡royaltalens.com](https://www.royaltalens.com/blogs/colour-stories/magenta#:~:text=Magenta%20is%20now%20an%20essential,the%20Italian%20town%20of); widely used in 19th c. for fabrics until safer dyes came, but remains in use for Gram staining bacteria and as a chemical indicator. [oai_citation_attribution:71‡edu.rsc.org](https://edu.rsc.org/feature/the-battle-for-magenta/2020242.article#:~:text=Three%20years%20after%20the%20discovery,and%20is%20still%20used%20today)
in_use: Limited (still in some lab stains and special uses)
natural_sources: Oxidation of aniline and toluidine (discovered 1858 in France)

color_description: Bright red that turns blue in acid (pH indicator properties); was valued for ability to dye cotton directly without mordant.
history: One of the earliest direct cotton dyes; historically significant in dye chemistry and as a laboratory pH indicator, but withdrawn from commercial use due to health hazards.
natural_sources: Synthesized from benzidine and naphthalene sulfonic acids (1884)
not_used_reason: Carcinogenic (metabolizes to benzidine); replaced by safer dyes

color_description: Bright lemon yellow; highly water-soluble; used for yellow-green coloration in foods.
history: One of the most commonly used artificial food colorings since the mid-20th century; its use has been contentious with periodic bans or warnings in various countries.
natural_sources: Petroleum-derived intermediates (e.g., sulfanilic acid, etc.)
source: Synthetic azo dye (sulfonated pyrazolone azo compound)
toxicity: GRAS (though can cause allergic reaction; in aspirin-sensitive individuals; hyperactivity concerns in children)

color_description: Bright red pigment with a slight yellowish (orange) cast; very soluble; stable to heat and light.
history: Became the primary red food dye after older reds (Amaranth, Red #2) were banned; now ubiquitous in candies, soft drinks, and cosmetics globally [oai_citation_attribution:82‡en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allura_Red_AC#:~:text=Allura%20Red%20AC%20has%20previously,In%20Norway%20and).
natural_sources: Petroleum-derived chemicals (naphthalene derivatives)
source: Synthetic azo dye (diazo dye from naphthalene sulfonic acids)
toxicity: GRAS (in regulated doses; high intake may be linked to hyperactivity in children; was banned in some countries now allowed with warnings)

color_description: Vivid royal blue shade; imparts a bright blue to confections, drinks, etc.; can produce a green with Tartrazine.
history: One of the most widely used synthetic blue pigments in food, beverages, and cosmetics; ubiquitous in candy, sports drinks, cereals, ice creams, and packaged foods. Also used in scientific and biomedical research as a tracer dye ('blue dye'); certified for use in the US since 1969. [oai_citation_attribution:87‡en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brilliant_blue_FCF#:~:text=Brilliant%20blue%20FCF%20,considered%20nontoxic%20and%20safe%20for)
natural_sources: Derived from coal tar / petrochemical intermediates (introduced 1920s)
origin: Approved as food pigment in the US in 1929

USA (RCA etc. 1950s standards) (1929 approval US, widely by 1960s) [oai_citation_attribution:83‡en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brilliant_blue_FCF#:~:text=Brilliant%20blue%20FCF%20,considered%20nontoxic%20and%20safe%20for)
synthesis: Chemical synthesis from coal tar derivatives
toxicity: GRAS (not absorbed by gut; passes through; rare allergic reactions).

color_description: Bright red-orange luminescence at ~611 nm when excited by electrons.
history: Enabled red pixels in color CRT televisions and monitors for decades; an example of a physical luminescent pigment used in displays.
natural_sources: High-purity chemical precipitation of yttrium, europium compounds, fired into phosphor
not_used_reason: Replaced by flat-panel display technologies (LED/LCD)
toxicity: Low (phosphor sealed in tube; not an exposure risk)

color_description: Bright yellowish-green luminescence (~530 nm) under electron excitation; short persistence.
history: The primary green in CRT TV screens; also used in radar screens (early cathode ray tubes) as a common fluorescent material.
natural_sources: Fusion of zinc, sulfur and dopants in controlled atmosphere to form phosphor powder
not_used_reason: Replaced by modern displays
source: Zinc sulfide activated with copper (plus cadmium, aluminum coactivators)
toxicity: Low (though contains some cadmium in older formula)

color_description: Bright blue-cyan luminescence (~450 nm) with short persistence; gave CRTs their blue primary.
history: Standard blue phosphor in color television CRTs and many oscilloscopes; part of the trio enabling full-color TV in the 20th century.
natural_sources: Chemical precipitation then firing of ZnS with Ag doping
not_used_reason: Replaced by modern displays
source: Zinc sulfide activated with silver (and co-activators)

color_description: Highly pure spectral color emission, tunable by particle size (e.g., ~630 nm red for larger CdSe QDs, ~540 nm green for smaller QDs); seen as bright saturated color points in displays.
history: Represents the new class of 'physical' pigments used in cutting-edge displays; provides wide color gamut in QLED televisions and other nano-enabled display technologies.
natural_sources: Chemical synthesis in solution (organometallic precursors of Cd and Se) to form monodisperse nanocrystals
origin: Commercialized in South Korea, China in QLED TVs 2010s
source: Colloidal semiconductor nanocrystal (cadmium selenide core, zinc sulfide shell often)
synthesis: Colloidal hot-injection method (Murray et al. 1993 for CdSe QDs)
toxicity: Toxic if ingested/breathed (contains cadmium), but encapsulated in products.

color_description: Absorbs 99.965% of visible light, appearing as almost complete darkness; surfaces coated appear as a flat void of color.
history: The blackest material known; used in astronomy (to reduce stray light in telescopes) and famously in art controversies (Anish Kapoor's exclusive rights). Symbolizes extreme of pigment performance.
natural_sources: Chemical vapor deposition growth of carbon nanotubes
not_used_reason: Specialized application, proprietary
source: Forest of vertically aligned carbon nanotubes on substrate
toxicity: Unknown as coating (not generally available); nanotubes can be hazardous if inhaled in free form.

color_description: Very light bluish green (ISCC–NBS descriptor); distinctive robin's egg blue shade associated with luxury jewelry brand Tiffany & Co.
history: First used in 1845 on the cover of Tiffany's Blue Book; became the signature color of the brand's packaging; registered as a color trademark in 1998; the PMS number 1837 references the year of Tiffany's foundation
origin: United States (1845, first used on Tiffany's Blue Book cover)
Registered as a color trademark in 1998
synthesis: Custom formulation by Pantone (PMS 1837), details proprietary
toxicity: Not applicable (trademarked color; not a chemical pigment)

color_description: Vivid transparent magenta-red with excellent lightfastness and clarity; can range from pinkish rose to deep maroon depending on particle form. Often labeled as 'Quinacridone Rose' or 'Quinacridone Magenta' depending on the hue variant.
history: Revolutionized artists' reds in the mid-20th century as a lightfast replacement for alizarin; also widely used in automotive paints and printing inks.
natural_sources: Derived from coal tar intermediates (discovered in 1958 by DuPont)

chemical_name: Proprietary formula (likely fluorescent dyes on synthetic substrate)
color_description: Intensely bright fluorescent pink; described as the 'pinkest' commercially available pink pigment powder
history: Created in 2016 by artist Stuart Semple in response to Anish Kapoor's exclusive rights to Vantablack. Became famous through the art world controversy when Semple banned Kapoor from purchasing it, making it available to everyone except Kapoor as a statement about art material accessibility.
origin: United Kingdom (2016, created by artist Stuart Semple)
synthesis: Proprietary formulation by Stuart Semple; likely uses fluorescent dyes on synthetic carrier
toxicity: Low toxicity; safe for art use but not cosmetic applications

color_description: Deep sky-blue to azure blue; notable for its luminescent properties (absorbs visible light and emits infrared radiation)
history: The first known synthetic pigment; used extensively in ancient Egyptian art, Roman frescoes, and throughout the Near East; its production technique was lost during the Middle Ages and only rediscovered in the 20th century through archaeological research
not_used_reason: Historical pigment, now mainly used in conservation and historical art reproduction
origin: Used throughout the ancient Mediterranean world
synthesis: Ancient Egyptian process involving copper compounds, calcium carbonate (lime), silica (quartz sand), and natron (sodium carbonate) heated to 800-900°C

color_description: Vibrant light blue with a slight turquoise quality; differs from Han Purple in being a true blue rather than purple; structurally related to Egyptian Blue but with barium instead of calcium
history: Ancient Chinese pigment discovered alongside Han Purple; used in tomb decorations, ceramics, and other artifacts; demonstrates the sophisticated chemical knowledge of ancient Chinese artisans; its formulation is similar to Egyptian Blue but was developed independently
not_used_reason: Historical pigment, not commercially produced for modern paints
origin: China (originated during Han Dynasty, 206 BCE-220 CE)
synthesis: Ancient Chinese process similar to Han Purple production, involving barium minerals, copper minerals, and quartz heated to high temperatures

color_description: Intensely dark blue-violet pigment with high tinting strength; in masstone appears nearly blackish purple, in tints gives bright violet.
history: Provided artists and industries a very strong, lightfast purple; replaced less stable mixtures; used in paints, plastics, printer toners, etc.
natural_sources: Derived from carbazole coal-tar chemical, first commercialized in 1950s

color_description: Transparent golden yellow with high tinting strength; somewhat unstable in watercolor (darkens over time)
history: Introduced in the 19th century and used by Impressionist painters; gradually fell out of favor due to its cost and issues with long-term stability
not_used_reason: Expensive and largely replaced by more lightfast alternatives
origin: Used in artists' palettes in 19th-early 20th century
synthesis: Precipitation of cobalt salt with potassium nitrite

color_description: Brilliant opaque lemon to orange-yellow; excellent hiding power but prone to darkening over time
history: Popular in 19th century painting (famously used by Vincent van Gogh); gradually replaced by cadmium yellows and modern alternatives due to toxicity concerns
not_used_reason: Toxicity (contains lead and hexavalent chromium)
origin: France (developed by Louis Nicolas Vauquelin, early 1800s)
Widely used in 19th century art and industrial applications
source: Lead chromate mineral (crocoite) or synthetic equivalent
synthesis: Precipitation of lead salt with potassium chromate solution
toxicity: Highly toxic (contains both lead and hexavalent chromium)
type: Both (natural mineral exists but pigment typically synthetic)

color_description: Bright yellowish green; varies in shade from yellowish to bluish depending on the ratio of components
history: Common in 19th century house paints and commercial applications; not to be confused with chromium oxide green (a different, safer pigment); largely obsolete today due to toxicity and availability of safer alternatives
not_used_reason: Toxicity (contains lead and hexavalent chromium)
origin: Used widely in commercial paints through early 20th century
source: Mixture of chrome yellow and Prussian blue
synthesis: Co-precipitation or physical mixture of chrome yellow and Prussian blue
toxicity: Highly toxic (contains lead and hexavalent chromium)

color_description: Deep azure blue that can range from light sky blue to deep navy depending on particle size; tends to convert to green malachite over time
history: One of the most important blue pigments in European painting before ultramarine; widely used in medieval and Renaissance art but gradually replaced by more stable synthetic blues
natural_sources: Azurite mineral (often found with malachite in copper deposits)
not_used_reason: Rare and expensive; less stable than modern synthetic blues
origin: Used in ancient Egypt and throughout Asia
Primary blue pigment in European Renaissance painting

color_description: Bright, opaque, warm yellow with excellent covering power; chemically stable but contains toxic lead
history: Important yellow pigment in European paintings from 1300-1750; mysteriously fell out of use and was 'rediscovered' by art conservators in the 20th century; appears in works by Vermeer, Raphael and other Old Masters
not_used_reason: Historical pigment; no longer produced due to lead toxicity
origin: Europe (used from 13th to 18th centuries, especially in Italian Renaissance painting)
synthesis: Heating lead and tin oxides together

color_description: Pale, cool lemon yellow with moderate opacity; less brilliant than chrome yellow but safer (though still toxic)
history: Used in 19th-early 20th century painting; also used as industrial corrosion inhibitor for metals; fell out of favor due to fugitive nature and toxicity
not_used_reason: Toxicity (contains hexavalent chromium) and poor lightfastness
synthesis: Precipitation of zinc compounds with chromate solution

color_description: Reddish-violet with moderate tinting strength; cooler and less intense than cobalt violet but more affordable
history: Introduced in the late 19th century as a more permanent alternative to fugitive organic purples; used by Post-Impressionist painters; remains in use in artist paints
synthesis: Complex reaction of manganese compounds with ammonium and phosphate

color_description: Light, cool yellow with greenish undertones; extremely stable to light and heat; good opacity
history: Developed as a non-toxic alternative to chrome and cadmium yellows; primarily used in industrial applications requiring heat stability (ceramics, plastics) but also available in some artist paints
synthesis: High-temperature solid state reaction of metal oxides

chemical_name: Mixture of zinc sulfide and barium sulfate
color_description: Warm white with less opacity than titanium white but softer optical properties; can darken slightly in intense light
history: Important industrial white pigment of the late 19th and early 20th centuries; cheaper alternative to lead white before titanium white became widespread; used in house paints, artist paints, and as a paper brightener
not_used_reason: Largely replaced by titanium white for most applications
origin: France (patented by J.G. Constant de Douhet in 1874)
source: Co-precipitated zinc sulfide and barium sulfate
synthesis: Co-precipitation of zinc sulfide with barium sulfate (chemical reaction of zinc sulfate and barium sulfide)
toxicity: Low (though historical formulations might contain trace heavy metals)

color_description: Deep maroon red with subtle brown undertone; very lightfast and opaque; excellent alternative to some cadmium or alizarin deep reds.
history: One of the modern synthetic organic pigments expanding the range of stable deep reds for artists and automotive paints in the late 20th century.
natural_sources: Derived from anthracene (coal tar) chemistry, developed mid-20th c.

color_description: Deep navy blue with moderate transparency; extremely lightfast and resistant to chemicals; less intense but more permanent than phthalo blue
history: Originally developed as a textile dye, Indanthrone became an important artist pigment in the mid-20th century when made into a lake; provides a more subdued alternative to phthalocyanine blue in artist palettes
origin: Germany (BASF, developed by René Bohn in 1901)
First truly lightfast blue vat dye
synthesis: Complex synthesis from anthraquinone derivatives (first made in 1901)

color_description: Soft, muted bluish-green with moderate tinting strength; more transparent than viridian
history: Historically significant as one of the first stable inorganic green pigments but never achieved widespread use due to high cost and relatively weak color; appears in some Impressionist works before being supplanted by cheaper alternatives
not_used_reason: Expensive; largely replaced by chromium oxide and phthalocyanine greens
synthesis: High-temperature calcination of cobalt and zinc compounds
